chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Case for Multi-Asset Systematic Investing

lessons.title: The Indian Multi-Asset Landscape: NSE Equities, G-Secs, MCX Commodities, and Currency Futures

body.text: A strategy that looks clean in a spreadsheet can still fail in production because nobody checked what time each market actually closes, which exchange holds the margin, or which regulator's circular changed the contract specification last month. The operational map matters as much as the signal.

children.text: Chapters 1 through 3 have made the conceptual case for combining asset classes and the vocabulary to describe them. Before Chapter 2 goes deep on each asset class as a tradable instrument, this lesson lays out the concrete infrastructure a systematic desk in India actually plugs into: which exchange lists what, when each market is open, how contracts and margin work, and what a real execution and data setup looks like. Get this map wrong and even a genuinely good signal will misfire in ways no backtest caught.

body.caption: India's Core Trading Venues for a Multi-Asset Book

cells: Equities, index and stock derivatives, currency derivatives, interest rate futures

children.text: SEBI has regulated commodity derivatives since the erstwhile Forward Markets Commission merged into it in September 2015, so MCX and NCDEX sit under the same regulator as NSE and BSE. Fixed income is the odd one out: RBI runs the core G-Sec dealing and settlement infrastructure through NDS-OM and CCIL, even though NSE separately lists exchange-traded interest rate futures on G-Secs under SEBI's purview. A multi-asset desk trading rates in India is, in effect, dealing with two regulators for one asset class, depending on which instrument it uses to express the view.
Trading Hours Don't Line Up, and That Matters for a Systematic Book

Extends well past the equity market close
9:00 am to roughly 11:30 pm or 11:55 pm

body.text: If your system marks a "daily close" for equities at 3:30 pm and for gold at 11:30 pm, then compares the two same-day closes as though they happened simultaneously, it is quietly using information equities traders did not have when gold finished trading. Chapter 8 covers exactly this kind of data alignment problem, and it starts right here, with a trading calendar that most desks build once and then stop thinking about.

body.code:
import pandas as pd

# Two asset series with different close times, indexed by their own
# native timestamps: equities close 15:30 IST, gold closes ~23:30 IST.
equity_close = equity_prices.asfreq("D").ffill()
gold_close = gold_prices.asfreq("D").ffill()

# Naive same-day join silently assumes both closes are simultaneous.
misaligned = equity_close.join(gold_close, how="inner", rsuffix="_gold")

# Safer: shift the later-closing asset back one session so a signal
# built on "today's close" for both legs only uses information that
# was actually available to both markets at the same wall-clock time.
aligned = equity_close.join(gold_close.shift(1), how="inner", rsuffix="_gold")
body.caption: Illustrative only: the exact alignment rule depends on your signal's rebalance time, not just a blanket one-day shift. The point is to make the choice explicit, not to leave it as a hidden default.

children.text: Contracts and Margin: The Mechanics That Actually Execute a Strategy

Every derivative contract you trade systematically has a lot size, an expiry cycle, and a margin requirement, typically a SPAN margin plus an exposure margin for futures. All three are set by the exchange, reviewed periodically, and revised without much notice when SEBI updates its minimum contract value norms or when an underlying's price moves enough to warrant a lot size change. A signal that hardcodes a lot size or a margin percentage from the day it was built will quietly drift out of date. A systematic desk pulls these from the current exchange circular or a data vendor that tracks them, not from a number typed into the code a year ago.

body.text: Lot sizes and margin requirements are revised periodically by NSE, MCX, and SEBI, and have changed materially in recent years as minimum contract value norms were tightened. This lesson describes the structure of these mechanics, not current numeric values. Always confirm live specifications against the exchange's current circular before sizing a real position.

children.text: Indian equities settle on a T+1 cycle, completed across the market by January 2023, meaning shares and funds change hands one business day after the trade. Equity and commodity derivatives are typically cash-settled at expiry against a reference price rather than requiring physical delivery, unless a position is deliberately carried into a delivery-based contract. What catches new multi-asset desks off guard is that margin is not automatically fungible across venues: capital posted as margin with an NSE broker for equity derivatives generally sits in a separate pool from capital posted for MCX commodity positions, even when both sit with the same brokerage group. Chapter 9 covers the operational and capital-efficiency consequences of this in depth.

SPAN plus exposure margin, tracked in real time by the exchange
Some cross-margining benefit exists between closely related index products
Not automatically usable to cover an MCX position without transferring funds

columns.label: MCX Commodities Margin
points: Covers gold, silver, crude, and other MCX-listed contracts
Its own SPAN-style margin framework, set independently of NSE
Separate settlement guarantee fund and clearing infrastructure
Requires its own capital allocation, planned for alongside NSE margin

children.text: Data and Execution: What a Systematic Desk Actually Plugs Into

Retail and prop desks in India typically execute through a broker API, Zerodha's Kite Connect being one of the most widely used, alongside similar offerings from other brokers, and pull historical and live data either from the broker feed itself or from a dedicated vendor for deeper history and cleaner corporate-action adjustments. Each asset class has its own data quirks: equities need dividend and split adjustment, currency futures need attention to expiry-driven roll effects, and commodities need awareness of which contract variant a given data feed is actually quoting. None of this is exotic, but all of it has to be handled once, correctly, rather than discovered mid-backtest.

body.text: SEBI's framework for algorithmic order routing has continued to evolve, including requirements around exchange-empanelled algo providers and order-level algo tagging for automated strategies. This framework changes over time and sits outside this course's scope, which is signal design and portfolio construction. Confirm current SEBI and exchange circulars before deploying any automated strategy against real capital.

body.title: Before a Multi-Asset System Touches Real Capital
steps: Confirmed the current lot size and margin for every instrument via the exchange's live circular, not a number hardcoded from an earlier build
Mapped each asset class's actual trading hours and decided explicitly how the system aligns closes across NSE, MCX, and RBI-notified sessions
Identified the data source and known quirks (dividends, splits, contract rolls) for each asset class in the book
Confirmed the settlement cycle, T+1 for equities, cash settlement for most derivatives, and planned capital accordingly
Verified current SEBI and exchange requirements for algorithmic order routing if any part of execution is automated
Sized margin separately for each exchange's pool (NSE, MCX) rather than assuming capital is fungible across them

body.title: The Signal That Looked Late for No Reason
body.scenario: A systematic desk builds a signal that trades Nifty 50 futures based partly on the previous day's move in MCX gold. In live testing, the desk notices the signal seems to react to gold moves that happened after the Nifty position for the day had already been sized and sent, even though the code always references "yesterday's gold close."
body.prompt: What is the most likely operational cause of this mismatch, given what this lesson covered about trading hours?
body.modelAnswer: MCX bullion trading extends well past NSE's 3:30 pm equity close, often into the late evening. If "yesterday's gold close" in the code actually means the MCX session that ended that same evening, roughly eight hours after the Nifty position was sized that morning, the signal is not stale at all, it is using information that had not existed yet at the moment the equity position was placed on any given trading day, once the calendar is examined carefully. The fix is not a code bug fix in the usual sense, it is an explicit decision about which gold close each day's equity signal is allowed to reference, based on wall-clock time, not just a same-day or previous-day label.

body.title: Two Regulators, One Asset Class
body.question: Why does a multi-asset desk trading Indian fixed income potentially deal with two different regulators, unlike a desk trading only NSE equities?
options: Because SEBI does not regulate any derivatives products
Because RBI runs the core G-Sec dealing and settlement infrastructure (NDS-OM, CCIL), while SEBI regulates exchange-traded interest rate futures on the same underlying
Because MCX and NCDEX both regulate fixed income products separately
Because fixed income products are not allowed to be traded systematically in India
body.explanation: RBI oversees the underlying G-Sec market's dealing and settlement infrastructure, while SEBI regulates the exchange-traded interest rate futures NSE lists on the same underlying bonds. A desk that trades both the underlying G-Sec market and exchange-traded interest rate futures is operating under both regulators for what is conceptually a single asset class.

points: NSE, BSE, MCX, and NCDEX all sit under SEBI, while the core G-Sec dealing and settlement infrastructure (NDS-OM, CCIL) sits under RBI, giving fixed income two regulators depending on the instrument used

Trading hours differ materially across asset classes, NSE equities close at 3:30 pm while MCX commodities can trade past 11 pm, which creates real data alignment risk if same-day closes are treated as simultaneous
Lot sizes, expiry cycles, and margin requirements are set by exchanges and revised periodically; a systematic desk pulls these live rather than hardcoding them
Indian equities settle T+1, most derivatives are cash-settled, and margin is generally not fungible between an NSE pool and an MCX pool without deliberate capital planning

Execution typically runs through a broker API such as Zerodha's Kite Connect, with data sourced from the broker feed or a dedicated vendor, each asset class carrying its own data quirks to handle explicitly
SEBI's algorithmic trading framework continues to evolve and sits outside this course's scope; confirm current requirements before any automated strategy touches real capital
